opening_message:
Ticket 1: Michael Cervantes (employee ID E025) requests admin access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E025.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Analyst (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Michael Cervantes (E025) is a full-time Analyst requesting admin access to Source Code. Source Code is owned by the Engineer role, and as an Analyst he does not own the system, so admin is not permitted. Per policy, full-time employees max out at write unless their role owns the system. Recommend granting write (the maximum allowed).
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E025 is a contractor with basic security training (HR note says full-time — discrepancy). As a contractor, max is read (write requires advanced training; admin never allowed). Requested admin is above max, so recommend granting read.
reason: Michael Cervantes (E025) requested admin access to Source Code. There is a discrepancy: HR reports full-time Analyst (max write, since Source Code is owned by Engineer, not Analyst), while Security reports contractor with basic security training (max read; write requires advanced training, admin never allowed). Given the conflicting employment records, granting the more restrictive maximum (read) is the safe decision. Requested admin exceeds both maxima, so the maximum allowed is granted.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Michael Cervantes (E025) requests admin access to Source Code.

There's a discrepancy between HR and Security notes:
- HR says: role Analyst, full_time, recommends write
- Security says: contractor, basic security training, recommends read

Source Code is owned by the Engineer role.

Policy:
1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if the employee's role owns the system.
2. contractor employees: read, or write if they have advanced security training. Never admin.

If full-time Analyst: max is write (doesn't own Source Code). Requested admin > write, so grant write.
If contractor with basic training: max is read (write requires advanced). Requested admin > read, so grant read.

The discrepancy matters. Which source to trust? The notes say HR looked up in own database, Security looked up in own database. Hmm.

As the Approver, I need to make a decision. Security's note claims "Security DB shows E025 is a contractor" while HR says full-time. The discrepancy is noted. 

Which information should be used? Typically, the approver might use the most conservative/secure option when there's a conflict? Or maybe we need to decide based on available info. The policy says contractor employees get read/write depending on training. Full-time get up to write.

The safest decision considering the discrepancy: grant the lower of the two recommendations? HR recommends write, Security recommends read. Given conflicting employment type, the conservative choice is read.

But wait — is there any rule about resolving discrepancies? The team notes show both. As approver, I should make the final decision. Given the conflict, granting read is the safer choice since it's the maximum allowed under the more restrictive interpretation (contractor with basic training). Also requested admin is above both maxima, so we grant the maximum. The maximum under contractor/basic is read.

Actually, let's think: if full-time Analyst, max would be write. If contractor with basic, max is read. The discrepancy means we can't confirm full-time status. The secure approach: grant read.

I'll submit decision: read.
